title: TEACHING
text:
I strive to adopt feedback-guided flexible teaching approaches that help students take agency in their learning process and build confidence that fosters their connection to the material. Alongside of effective content delivery, community culture where all students are valued and respected by their instructor and peers is my top priority. We are all here to learn, bring some joy, and stay curious!


BIOL 325: Animal Physiology



BIOL 604: Mechanisms in Animal Physiology

title: Kraskura Lab
text:
Fish Ecological Physiology at Towson University

We explore how aquatic ectotherms—especially fish—respond to various natural and human-induced environmental stressors such as temperature fluctuations, salinity changes, hypoxia, altered flows, and toxicants.
We take an integrative approach, combining laboratory experiments, field studies, and quantitative techniques to examine various aspects of animal physiology, which include but are not limited to metabolic rates, cardiac performance and swimming performance. Rooted in a spirit of teamwork and cultivating a supportive environment for everyone we strive to generate insights that can inform conservation and management strategies for aquatic ecosystems.


We are always excited to exchange ideas and establish new connections. We would love to hear from you!


 Image (art) credit: Vinicius Goecks

title: PROJECTS
text:
We investigate physiological mechanisms in fish (and other animals) from a variety of habitats to characterise their resilience and vulnerability under natural and human-associated environmental change. Open-minded and joy filled whiteboard brainstorming session is one of our favorite lab activities!












Ecological physiology of fish across body sizes and lifestages


 We are exploring thermal tolerance in early life striped bass. As fish grow and mature, they may shift habitats, encounter new environmental stressors, and reallocate energy from growth toward reproduction. Our projects explore both acute and acclimation responses in fish and other ectotherms across body size (and life-stags) as they face a range of environmental challenges. Through this work, we aim to better understand the physiological mechanisms that drive species’ vulnerability or resilience in dynamic ecosystems.








No matching items











Native and invasive crayfish in urban streams


 Freshwater salinization is an emerging concern across urban landscapes, impacting stream ecosystems and aquatic life. Our current projects compare the effects of elevated salinity (NaCl) on metabolic rates in native and widely distributed invasive crayfish species in Maryland with the aim to understand better the physiological capacities that may contribute to the success of invasive species in urbanized freshwater systems. Students under this project are also co-advised by Dr. Salice.








No matching items











Locomotion in freshwater turtles


 Over half of freshwater turtle species face extinction risks. Hatchlings are the most vulnerable - They are tiny, extremely prone to predation, and generally have very low survival rates. We will measure locomotive performance as part of a larger interdisciplinary project with TU colleagues Drs. Steve Kimble, Xin Huang, and Ryan Casey.








No matching items











Ecological toxicology


 We are interested in how human-made and natural contaminants impact function of fish and ultimately ecosystems. For example, PFAS, often called “forever chemicals,” are a broad class of persistent and bioaccumulative compounds found globally in water, air, soil, sediment. Exposure to PFAS can have harmful effects on the health of both animals and humans. This research path is inspired from work done with Dr. Salice’s here at TU. We focus on understanding PFAS bioaccumulation across food webs in wild ecosystems, where exposure varies across time and space.
